lessons.title: Hazards in the packhouse and your rights and duties
lessons.html:
The law and you

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (OHS Act) protects people at work. Your employer must provide a safe workplace, safe machines, training, and the protective equipment you need. You, the worker, must:

  • Follow safety rules and instructions.
  • Use the protective equipment you are given.
  • Not interfere with or misuse safety equipment.
  • Report unsafe conditions and every injury to your supervisor or health and safety representative as soon as possible.

Workplaces have health and safety representatives chosen from the workers. They help check safety and listen to workers' concerns.

Common packhouse hazards

HazardExample
Moving machineryBelts, rollers, chains, carton machines, strapping machines
Forklifts and pallet jacksBeing hit or crushed; falling loads
Slips and tripsWet floors, fruit on the floor, loose straps
ChemicalsFruit treatments, waxes, cleaning chemicals
NoiseSizers, compressors, fans
ColdWorking in cold rooms
Lifting and repetitive workBack strain, sore wrists and shoulders
ElectricityDamaged cables, wet electrical panels
FireCardboard stores, electrical faults, gas forklifts

Safety signs

Learn the signs: red circles mean prohibited, yellow triangles warn of danger, blue circles mean you must do something (wear PPE), and green signs show safe conditions such as exits and first aid.

Health hazards you cannot see

Not all hazards cause an injury straight away. Loud noise every day slowly damages hearing, and the damage cannot be repaired. Breathing chemical fumes or dust over months can harm the lungs. Standing for long hours and repeating the same movement thousands of times can cause pain in the back, wrists and shoulders. These are called occupational health hazards. Your employer may arrange medical checks, such as hearing tests, for workers in noisy areas. Tell your supervisor or the health and safety representative early if you notice pain, ringing in the ears or breathing problems, so the cause can be found and fixed.

lessons.title: Working safely and responding to emergencies
lessons.html:
Personal protective equipment (PPE)

Wear the PPE given for your job: safety shoes, hearing protection near noisy machines, gloves and goggles for chemicals, warm clothing in cold rooms, and high-visibility vests where forklifts work. Check PPE before use, keep it clean and ask for a replacement if it is damaged.

Safe work rules

  • Never reach into moving machines. Keep guards in place.
  • Only trained and authorised people may repair or clear machines, using lockout procedures.
  • Walk only in marked walkways. Make eye contact with forklift drivers. Never ride on forklifts.
  • Pick up fruit and straps from the floor; report spills and wet floors.
  • Lift correctly: feet apart, bend your knees, keep your back straight and the load close, do not twist. Ask for help with heavy loads.
  • Change position, stretch, and use anti-fatigue mats where you stand for long periods.
  • Never mix chemicals. Read the label and safety data sheet.
  • Do not come to work under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

Fire

  • Know where the fire extinguishers, hose reels, alarms and exits are.
  • Keep exits and fire equipment clear, never blocked by pallets or cartons.
  • Smoke only in the marked smoking area.
  • If there is a fire, raise the alarm, leave by the nearest exit and go to the assembly point. Only use an extinguisher if you are trained and it is safe.

Injuries and first aid

If someone is injured: make the area safe (for example press the emergency stop), call the first aider and your supervisor, and do not move a seriously injured person unless they are in danger. Every injury, even a small cut, must be reported and recorded. Injured workers may be able to claim under the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA). First aid is only given by trained first aiders; hands-on training by an accredited provider is required.

Evacuation

When the evacuation alarm sounds, stop work, switch off machines if it is safe, walk (do not run) to the assembly point and wait to be counted. Never go back inside until told it is safe.

Key points

  • The OHS Act 85 of 1993 gives duties to both employer and worker.
  • Know the hazards: machines, forklifts, slips, chemicals, noise, cold, lifting and fire.
  • Wear your PPE and follow safe work rules.
  • Report every injury and unsafe condition.
  • Know the exits, fire equipment and assembly point.
